page.text:
The transition from real multivariable calculus to complex analysis is marked by an
extraordinary tightening of differentiability. In multivariable calculus on $\mathbb{R}^2$,
a mapping $F(x, y) = (u(x,y), v(x,y))$ is differentiable at $(x_0, y_0)$ if its increments
are linearly approximated by a total derivative represented by an arbitrary $2 \times 2$
real Jacobian matrix:
$$ DF(x_0, y_0) = \begin{pmatrix} u_x & u_y \\ v_x & v_y \end{pmatrix}. $$
Such a linear operator has four independent degrees of freedom; it can stretch different
directions by different ratios and shear angles between intersecting curves.

In complex analysis, by contrast, a function $f: U \to \mathbb{C}$ is complex differentiable
if the limit of the difference quotient
$$ f'(z_0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(z_0 + h) - f(z_0)}{h} $$
exists as a single complex number $a + ib$. Because multiplication by $a + ib$ corresponds
in $\mathbb{R}^2$ to the rotation-dilation matrix
$$ \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix}, $$
the requirement of complex differentiability constrains the four entries of the Jacobian matrix
to satisfy $u_x = v_y = a$ and $u_y = -v_x = -b$. These are the celebrated *Cauchy--Riemann equations*.
This single geometric constraint forces $DF(x_0, y_0)$ to be an orientation-preserving similarity,
preserving all angles and scaling all infinitesimal tangent directions equally. From this local
isotropy springs the entire majestic rigidity of holomorphic functions.
